name: USeW World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The federation's own top belt, and one a returning legend claimed on air had only been renamed: the JCWF's own world title, he said, carried under new letters since the merger that swallowed his federation. It changed hands twice in twenty-two days in the spring of 1996 — taken off 187 at Leprecharnage with a chair slid in by that same returning legend, and taken back on the next Blow-Out in a match the federation's own president cleared both entourages out of, to see who the better man was. Its earlier line is only partly recoverable: a 600-pound champion in May 1995, and a masked former champion out of Guadalajara still being billed as one a year later.
notes: The claim that it was formerly the JCWF's own championship is made on air by Freddy Flame at Leprecharnage and is not corroborated elsewhere in the held record: “you can change the name of the title, but that doesn't mean a two bit thug can still wear it.” Recorded as the fed's own on-air claim, not as an established lineage.

name: USeW World Television Championship
epitaph: Made in early 1996 out of the North American title's own abolition — a four-way match for a new belt, on a night the federation said it wanted to be more competitive — and then the most-travelled championship in the surviving record: three changes in thirty-six days, to a visiting EWF light heavyweight at Leprecharnage, to a masked former world champion three weeks later in three minutes, and to a trumpet-carrying former light heavyweight champion three weeks after that.
notes: The federation's own account of the four-way that created the belt contradicts itself inside a single sentence — it names Haplo as the reigning Television champion at the time AND Justice D. Nyde as the current World Television champion, then says Haplo retained — while every other document bills Nyde as the champion going into Leprecharnage. The contradiction is recorded rather than resolved, and no reign is written for that match.

name: USeW World Television Tag Team Championship
epitaph: A second set of tag belts below the World Tag Team titles, and the busiest pair in the federation's own spring: held by a card-sharp team whose manager kept them at Leprecharnage by getting his own men disqualified, taken three weeks later by two masked giants in a twenty-nine-minute match, and kept a fortnight after that by exactly the same trick in reverse.
aka: USeW World TV Tag Team Championship

name: USeW World Tag Team Championship
epitaph: The federation's own senior tag championship. Two reigns survive and neither of their beginnings does: brothers holding it in May 1995 with a mini-tournament booked to decide their next challengers, and an undefeated pair out of London holding it a year later and finishing their Leprecharnage defence in three minutes thirty-six.

name: USeW Light-Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The belt the federation's own smaller men fought over, and the one whose defences the record catches at their least ordinary: a champion branded with a hot iron before his own title match and saved by a magician, and, a year later, a rookie who asked for a match with one of the sport's best high flyers to prove something to himself and shook hands with him afterwards.

name: USeW United States Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: One reign survives, and it was new when the record catches it: a newly crowned champion in May 1995, already booked into the World Heavyweight title match that was to close the card.

name: USeW North American Championship
epitaph: Abolished in its own champion's hands. He was stripped of it in February 1996 for two reasons the federation gave at once — that he had begun calling it the Native American Title, and that the federation wanted to be more competitive — and the president then announced the championship would no longer exist, replacing it with a four-way match for a new Television title. Its former holders wrestled on for months billed as former North American champions.
notes: Justice D. Nyde is separately named on the same broadcast as another former North American champion.

events.note: Abolished by the federation's own president in the announcement that stripped Comanche War Dog and opened a four-way match for the new World Television Title. Dated from the Leprecharnage broadcast of 17 March 1996, which places it “three weeks ago.”
